recentItems.title: Inside Russia: Young people voting against Putin's war in Ukraine
recentItems.description:
Russians will be heading to the polls for parliamentary elections this weekend, and perhaps unsurprisingly Vladimir Putin’s United Russia party is leading as the war in Ukraine continues.

[Subscribe to our Substack newsletter: https://channel4news.substack.com/subscribe]

So is there still a political pulse in a nation where Putin rules supreme and parties that oppose the war are banned? 

Voters will go to the polls over three days to elect a new State Duma in the first parliamentary elections since Russia's full scale invasion of Ukraine. 

The only anti-war party has been banned, while candidates deemed to have "undesirable" opinions have been disqualified or jailed. 

This is a rare journey through Moscow, where we discover what campaigning looks like in an election where everyone already knows who the winner will be. 

Producer: Millicent Teasdale
Editor: Kristy Jane Breetzke

recentItems.title: Trump lashes out as EU seeks closer ties with Canada
recentItems.description:
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has welcomed a plan to make Canada the EU’s first “associate member”. But it hasn’t gone down well with Donald Trump.

[Subscribe to our Substack newsletter: https://channel4news.substack.com/subscribe]

Carney declared to the European Parliament that his country and Europe are “stronger together” as he tries to fashion a new world order.

While Trump threatened to impose "very serious" tariffs if the partnership went ahead, Carney insisted that no one could tell his country who they could strike agreements with. 

Freedom and sovereignty were at stake, he said, in a speech that sounded more like a declaration of independence.

recentItems.title: Netanyahu moves to strip Israeli filmmakers of citizenship over Gaza documentary
recentItems.description:
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu says he wants to introduce new laws that could strip citizenship from people who “defame” Israeli soldiers or the state.

[Subscribe to our Substack newsletter: https://channel4news.substack.com/subscribe]

The move comes after Israeli filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor faced intense backlash over their documentary NAZA.

The film takes its title from an acronym reportedly used by the Israeli intelligence service for expected “collateral casualties”.

It alleges “mass killing of Palestinian civilians in Gaza” was "calculated" by Israeli military personnel, according to the official synopsis. 

The Israeli government rejects those accusations. 

NAZA recently just received a special jury prize and an unprecedented 25 minute long standing ovation at the Venice Film Festival.

The directors have also faced threats from Israeli ultra-nationalist groups while more than 1,500 Israeli filmmakers have signed a petition supporting them and freedom of expression.

recentItems.title: Could AI really ‘kill us all’? - Warnings explained
recentItems.description:
What is going on with AI? Some of the most influential people in the world have warned its development must slow down - and that humanity risks extinction.

Even King Charles warned an AI summit about “adequately considering the existential dangers of such technologies falling into the wrong hands, and being used in potentially catastrophic ways".

It comes just days after a researcher at Anthropic, the company behind the Claude chatbot, quit after a bombshell post warning that colleagues believed AI could “kill us all by the end of the decade”.

Anthropic says it continues to build some of the strongest safeguards in the industry.
In the wake of these warnings, many have called for regulation to be put in place.
But keeping AI safe comes at a cost - and America doesn’t want to fall behind in the tech race.

Earlier this week, President Donald Trump posted on his Truth Social platform that the fears were “a hoax”.

In this episode of the breakdown, we examine how dangerous AI could become, what effective regulation might look like and whether the world could ever agree on the rules needed to keep it under control.
We put those questions to journalist and author Sebastian Mallaby - whose latest book charts the rise of the Google DeepMind research lab and its CEO.

-------

Presenter: Ayshah Tull
Producers: Tyler Anderson, Harry Peet
Series Producer: Joseph Keith

recentItems.title: Can Trump block Canada's Europe alliance?
recentItems.description:
The EU President Ursula Von der Leyen has offered Canada ‘associate membership of the EU’, a move which Donald Trump called ‘laughable’ - but still threatened ‘serious sanctions’ as punishment.  

[Subscribe to our Substack newsletter: https://channel4news.substack.com/subscribe]

In this episode of the Fourcast, we ask what Canada’s closer ties with the EU could mean - from tighter trade and defense to what Mark Carney calls 'a beacon for other democracies.' But with the far right rising in Europe, is the Canadian Prime Minister trying to join a club that could soon fall apart?  

Leslie Vinjamuri, the President and CEO of the Chicago Council on Global Affairs says Carney is playing a long-game when it comes to the US, picking up support on both sides of the border by standing up to Trump, and that his decision to move closer to the EU is a ‘declaration of independence from King Trump’.  While Dr. Linn Selle, head of the Europe division of the German Council on Foreign Relations, argues that the EU is chasing Carney’s star power to help revive its appeal.

recentItems.title: How DEI became a divisive political battleground
recentItems.description:
When academic and writer Jason Arday became the youngest Black professor at Cambridge he fulfilled an ambition he'd set himself as a young man. But from the start, there were those who questioned his right to be there. 

[Subscribe to our Substack newsletter: https://channel4news.substack.com/subscribe]

His work and his personal life came under intense scrutiny, at a time when DEI became a defining front in a transatlantic culture war. Last month he was found dead at his home. A month on, his story sits at the heart of a much wider question -  how did DEI become such a divisive political battleground?
